claims.text: TaVCrW is a disordered body-centered-cubic solid solution at 0 K.
Replacing EAM and TI with a TaVCrW-trained MTP and FEP will reduce computational cost by more than 80%.
The MTP-FEP result will remain within 0.5 meV/atom in free energy of the TOR-TILD result.
Short-range order contributes approximately 2-3 meV/atom of stabilization energy in TaVCrW.
Accurate FEP requires the MTP to reproduce the ab initio phase-space distributions of both the complex liquid and solid.
The MTP can capture the electronic density of states near the Fermi level.
A TaVCrW MTP can serve as an accurate, computationally efficient surrogate for the DFT energy landscape.
Using the MTP allows FEP to sample phase space directly without the slow convergence associated with TI.
FEP converges faster than TI when the reference and target systems differ only by a small perturbation.
The MTP has linear computational scaling relative to DFT.
More than 1000 atoms are typically required to estimate SRO energies accurately in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The 2000-2400 K range is sufficient to fully sample the TaVCrW liquid phase.
Finite-temperature DFT configurations in the training set would enable the MTP to include electronic-excitation effects.
High-temperature magnetic fluctuations may alter the TaVCrW free-energy landscape and shift its melting point by tens of kelvin.
Empirical GGA-PBE/LDA underbinding and overbinding rules do not hold for V and Cr at 0 K.
DFT errors involving V and Cr may propagate into an MTP trained on those DFT data.
FEP accuracy depends strongly on overlap between the reference and target phase-space distributions.
Insufficient diversity of liquid configurations in the MTP training set can cause the method to fail.
A 2000-atom benchmark supercell is sufficient to ensure that SRO is captured.
